passages.title: How the Brain Learns a Second Language
passages.text:
Learning a second language as an adult is hard. Children seem to learn languages without effort, but adults often struggle for years and still make mistakes. Scientists who study the brain want to know why this is, and what adults can do to learn better.
The main reason children learn languages easily is that their brains are still developing. In the first years of life, the brain makes millions of new connections between its cells, and it is very good at noticing patterns in the sounds it hears. A baby can hear the difference between sounds in any language in the world, but by the age of one, the baby has learned to ignore the sounds that do not matter in its own language.
Adults have lost some of this flexibility, but they have not lost the ability to learn. The adult brain can still make new connections, and it can still learn new words and new rules. The difference is that adults learn more slowly, and they need more practice to make the new language automatic.
One important discovery is that the brain treats a second language differently from the first. When a person uses their first language, the brain uses areas that are well practised and work quickly. When the same person uses a second language, the brain uses more areas, including areas that control attention and memory. This is why speaking a second language can feel tiring: the brain is working harder.
Another discovery is that sleep plays an important role in learning a language. During sleep, the brain replays what it learned during the day, and it moves new words from short-term memory to long-term memory. Studies have shown that people who sleep after a language lesson remember more words the next day than people who stay awake.
Scientists have also found that the best way to learn a language is to use it in real situations. Reading a list of words is less effective than using the words in a conversation, because the brain remembers words better when they are linked to a meaning and an experience. This is why children learn their first language so well: they use it all day, every day, to get what they want.
There is also good news for adults. People who learn a second language, even as adults, have brains that stay healthier for longer. Studies of older people have shown that those who speak two languages develop dementia, a disease that affects memory, about four years later than people who speak only one language. Learning a language, it seems, is good exercise for the brain.
There has been much debate about the best age to learn a language. Some scientists believe that there is a critical period, before the age of about twelve, after which it becomes much harder to speak a new language without an accent. Others say that adults can learn just as well, and that the difference is not age but time: children spend thousands of hours using their first language, while adults usually study for only a few hours a week.
Children who grow up with two languages often mix them, using a word from one language in a sentence in the other. Parents sometimes worry about this, but scientists say it is normal, and it is not a sign of confusion. Bilingual children usually separate the two languages by the time they start school, and they often develop a better understanding of how language works than children who speak only one language.
Technology is changing how adults learn languages. Apps on a phone can teach new words, correct pronunciation, and let learners practise with speakers in other countries. But scientists warn that an app alone is not enough. Language is learned by using it with other people, and no app can replace a real conversation. The best results come from combining technology with real practice: using an app to learn words, and then using the words with a real person.
The advice from scientists is simple. If you want to learn a language, use it every day, even for a short time. Listen, speak, read and write. Sleep well after you study. And do not worry about making mistakes: mistakes are a sign that your brain is learning.

From Monday 1 September, the swimming pool will open at 7.00 am on weekdays, one hour earlier than before. On Saturdays, the pool will open at 8.00 am, and on Sundays at 9.00 am. The pool closes at 9.00 pm every day. Children under the age of eight must be accompanied by an adult at all times. A family ticket, for two adults and up to three children, costs £18.
TEXT B — MARKET SQUARE CAR PARK
The car park in Market Square will be closed on Sunday 14 September for the annual food festival. Drivers should use the car park on Station Road instead. The Station Road car park is open 24 hours a day, and the first hour is free. Please note that cars left in Market Square car park after 6.00 pm on Saturday 13 September will be removed.
TEXT C — EVENING CLASSES AT THE COMMUNITY CENTRE
New evening classes begin in October. Classes include Spanish for beginners on Mondays, photography on Tuesdays, and yoga on Thursdays. All classes run from 7.00 pm to 9.00 pm, and cost £60 for a ten-week course. To book a place, please call 01632 960444 or visit the community centre office, which is open from 9.00 am to 5.00 pm, Monday to Friday.
TEXT D — LOST PROPERTY: BLUE BICYCLE
TEXT E — SATURDAY MARKET: NEW STALLHOLDERS WANTED
The Saturday market in Market Square is looking for new stallholders. Stalls are available from 8.00 am to 2.00 pm every Saturday. A stall costs £15 a day, and stallholders must bring their own table and cover. Anyone interested should contact the market manager, Mrs Allen, on 01632 960511, before Friday 26 September.
TEXT F — BUS STOP CLOSURE
The bus stop outside the library will be closed from Monday 22 September to Friday 26 September, while the pavement is repaired. During this time, buses will stop at the temporary stop on Church Street, about five minutes' walk away. Passengers are advised to allow extra time for their journeys.
A blue bicycle was found outside the library on Tuesday 9 September. The bicycle is now at the library reception desk. To collect it, please bring proof of ownership, such as a photograph of the bicycle or the key to its lock. The library is open from 9.00 am to 6.00 pm, Monday to Saturday.

passages.text:
TEXT A — STAFF HANDBOOK: WORKING HOURS
All staff are expected to arrive at work by 9.00 am. If you are going to be late, please phone your manager before 9.00 am. Lunch is for one hour, between 12.00 and 2.00 pm, and you may choose when to take it. The normal working day finishes at 5.30 pm. Staff who work more than two hours beyond their normal finishing time may claim a meal allowance of up to £10.
TEXT B — STAFF HANDBOOK: SICK LEAVE
If you are ill and cannot come to work, you must phone your manager before 9.30 am on the first day of your illness. If you are ill for more than three days, you must provide a note from your doctor. Staff are entitled to ten days of paid sick leave each year. Any sick leave beyond ten days will be unpaid, unless your manager agrees otherwise in writing.
TEXT C — NOTICE TO ALL STAFF: FIRE DRILL
There will be a fire drill on Wednesday 17 September at 11.00 am. When you hear the alarm, please leave the building at once by the nearest fire exit, and go to the assembly point in the car park. Do not use the lifts, and do not stop to collect personal belongings. Please remember that the fire exits must be kept clear at all times, and boxes must never be stored in the corridors.
TEXT D — STAFF CANTEEN: NEW MENU
TEXT E — STAFF SOCIAL CLUB: QUIZ NIGHT
The staff social club will hold a quiz night on Friday 26 September at 7.30 pm in the canteen. Teams of up to six people may enter, and the entry fee is £2 per person. There will be prizes for the winning team, and sandwiches will be provided. To enter a team, please write your names on the list on the noticeboard by Wednesday 24 September.
TEXT F — PARKING PERMITS
Staff who drive to work must display a parking permit on their car. Permits for the new year are available from the reception desk from Monday 29 September. Please bring your car registration number with you. Cars without a valid permit may be fined £25.
From next Monday, the staff canteen will offer a hot vegetarian meal every day, as well as a choice of sandwiches and salads. The canteen is open from 8.00 am to 3.00 pm, Monday to Friday. Tea and coffee are free for all staff, but other drinks must be paid for at the till.

passages.title: The Story of the Lighthouse
passages.text:
For hundreds of years, lighthouses have guided ships safely to shore. A lighthouse is a tall tower with a powerful light at the top, built on a dangerous coast or on rocks in the sea. Its light warns sailors of danger, and helps them to find their way into harbour at night or in bad weather.
The most famous lighthouse of the ancient world was the Pharos of Alexandria, in Egypt. It was built in about 280 BC, on a small island at the entrance to the harbour of Alexandria. The tower was about 120 metres high, which made it one of the tallest buildings in the ancient world. At night, a fire burned at the top of the tower, and its light could be seen from far out at sea. The Pharos stood for more than 1,500 years, until it was damaged by earthquakes and finally fell down in the fourteenth century.
For many centuries after the Pharos, few lighthouses were built. Ships usually stayed close to the coast during the day, and at night they dropped anchor and waited for morning. But as trade grew, ships began to sail at night and in all weathers, and the number of shipwrecks increased. By the seventeenth century, several European countries had begun to build lighthouses on their most dangerous coasts.
Early lighthouses used candles or oil lamps, which gave only a weak light. The light was improved in the nineteenth century, when a French scientist named Augustin Fresnel invented a special lens. The Fresnel lens collected the light from a lamp and sent it out in a powerful beam, which could be seen from more than 30 kilometres away. Fresnel lenses are still used in some lighthouses today.
Life for a lighthouse keeper was hard and lonely. Keepers lived in the lighthouse, often with their families, and their job was to keep the light burning all night, every night, in all weathers. They also had to clean the lens, paint the tower, and repair the building after storms. In remote lighthouses, keepers might not see another person for weeks, and supplies arrived by boat only once a month.
In the twentieth century, lighthouses began to change. Electric lights replaced oil lamps, and machines replaced the keepers. The last manned lighthouse in Britain was automated in 1998, and today almost all lighthouses are controlled by computers from far away. A lighthouse keeper is now a rare job.
Some people think that lighthouses are no longer needed, because ships now have satellite navigation systems that can show their exact position. But sailors still value lighthouses, because a satellite system can fail, and a light on the coast is a simple, reliable guide that needs no technology on the ship. Many old lighthouses have also found a new life: some are now museums, some are hotels, and some are homes.
One of the most famous lighthouses ever built stands on the Eddystone rocks, about 14 kilometres off the coast of Plymouth, in England. The rocks are covered by the sea at high tide, and many ships were wrecked there. The first lighthouse on the rocks, built of wood in 1698, was washed away by a great storm five years later. A second lighthouse, built of stone in 1709, was destroyed by fire. The third lighthouse, built in 1759, stood for more than a hundred years, and its design was copied all over the world.
Today, many lighthouses are open to visitors. People can climb the narrow stairs to the top, look out over the sea, and learn about the lives of the keepers who once lived there. Some lighthouses offer rooms where visitors can stay the night, and wake up to the sound of the sea. For many visitors, the most memorable part is the light itself: a beam that sweeps across the water, just as it has done for hundreds of years.
Lighthouses have also inspired writers and artists. The most famous lighthouse in literature is the one in Virginia Woolf's novel To the Lighthouse, published in 1927. In the novel, the lighthouse is a goal that the family hopes to reach, but the journey is delayed again and again. For Woolf, the lighthouse stood for something distant and difficult to reach, yet always shining in the distance, calling people towards it.
The lighthouse has become a symbol of safety and hope. It appears in paintings, in poems and in songs, as a light that guides people through the dark. Long after the last keeper has left, the light still shines.
